Storytelling challenge

Abandoned but not Forgotten

Since the 1960s, NASA has left machines all over the solar system. Some are parked on the Moon. Some went quiet on Mars. Some are still flying and still calling home. Meet them, then play.

Meet the gear Play the games

Where did it all go?

Pick a place. Every machine shows its status and when it last called home.

Built for a short trip. Stayed for years.

Engineers planned short missions for these Mars robots. Compare the plan with what really happened.

Spirit
Planned: 90 days
Worked: about 6 years
Opportunity
Planned: 90 days
Worked: about 14 years
InSight
Planned: about 2 years
Worked: about 4 years

Play the mission

Four games. Each one teaches you something about the gear NASA left behind.

Drive a rover across Mars. Tap the screen or press Space to jump. Dodge the rocks and grab the glowing samples. Every 3 samples, Mission Control sends you a fact.

Dust Dash

Help the rover collect samples before the sun sets.

Samples: 0Best: 0
Mission logCollect 3 samples to get your first message.

Fly a rocket from Earth to Mars, through a black hole, and into a boss fight. Drag with your finger, move the mouse, or use the arrow keys to steer. Dodge everything. Grab stars. Every 5 stars repair a heart.

Rocket Quest

Stage: 1 of 4Lives: ♥♥♥Stars: 0
Your missionYou are the young astronaut in this rocket. Blast off from Earth, visit Mars, slip through a black hole and meet the Junk King, guardian of the old space junk.

Explore music

Stars Are Calling

An original 2:58 sing-along song about exploring space, from the Moon and Mars to deep space. Sing the words as they light up. The beats and sounds circle your head in 8D, so put on headphones.

Made for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

The song "Stars Are Calling" is original music and lyrics made for this project.

This is a student project, not an official NASA website. Statuses were gathered at the time of writing. For the latest news, visit nasa.gov.
